pages.text: Half a kilometre past the new school, a dirt track led to Old Akokoaso, where Yakubu’s great-grandparents once lived. Nobody lived there now; it was abandoned. Children whispered that it was haunted: lights flickered, footsteps clicked, and a cold breath came from the doorways.
sentences: Half a kilometre past the new school, a dirt track led to Old Akokoaso, where Yakubu’s great-grandparents once lived.
Nobody lived there now; it was abandoned.
Children whispered that it was haunted: lights flickered, footsteps clicked, and a cold breath came from the doorways.
pages.alt: A dirt track leads towards ruined mud houses under a darkening sky.

pages.text: Yakubu and Adoma wanted the truth. Madam Gyan said, ‘First, we ask permission. The old village belongs to the community.’ The chief and elders agreed, with three rules: go with adults, enter no buildings, touch and take nothing.

The old village belongs to the community.’ The chief and elders agreed, with three rules: go with adults, enter no buildings, touch and take nothing.
pages.alt: Two children and a teacher speak respectfully to a chief and elders.

pages.text: Opanin Boakye, a retired teacher, walked them to the edge of the old village. They saw low mud walls, a tilted house with a rusty tin roof and a grinding stone. ‘When the new road was built on the other side of the hill,’ he said, ‘the shops, school and clinic moved there, and people followed. These were our families’ homes.’

pages.alt: An elder points out ruined mud walls and an old grinding stone to the children.

pages.text: The detectives listed the ghost clues and guessed natural causes. Lights: fireflies, or moonlight on broken glass. Footsteps: animals, or the tin roof. Cold breath: moving air. ‘A hypothesis is a guess we can test,’ said Adoma.
sentences: The detectives listed the ghost clues and guessed natural causes.
Lights: fireflies, or moonlight on broken glass.
Footsteps: animals, or the tin roof.
Cold breath: moving air.
‘A hypothesis is a guess we can test,’ said Adoma.
pages.alt: The children write three columns in a notebook: clue, guess, test.

pages.text: At dusk, they sat on a log at a safe distance with Opanin Boakye. As the sun went down, the old tin roof began to tick and click, as if someone was walking on it. ‘Metal shrinks a little as it cools,’ said Yakubu. He wrote the time: 6:20 p.m.

‘Metal shrinks a little as it cools,’ said Yakubu.
He wrote the time: 6:20 p.m.
pages.alt: The children sit on a log at dusk looking at a tin roof with the sun going down.

pages.text: Then hundreds of small shapes poured from a gap in the wall against the orange sky. ‘Bats,’ whispered Adoma. ‘They sleep in the ruins by day and fly out at dusk.’ Over the grass, little lights blinked on and off: fireflies. ‘Ghost lights,’ whispered Yakubu, and grinned.
sentences: Then hundreds of small shapes poured from a gap in the wall against the orange sky.
‘Bats,’ whispered Adoma.
‘They sleep in the ruins by day and fly out at dusk.’ Over the grass, little lights blinked on and off: fireflies.
‘Ghost lights,’ whispered Yakubu, and grinned.
pages.alt: Bats stream out of a broken wall while fireflies glow over the grass.

pages.text: A breeze moved through an empty doorway and made a low whoosh, like breathing. Adoma held up a strip of paper. It fluttered. ‘Moving air,’ she said. They did not laugh at the old stories. ‘Stories can be a way of saying: this place matters, be careful,’ said Opanin Boakye. ‘And old walls can fall. That is a real reason to keep out.’

‘And old walls can fall.

pages.alt: A strip of paper flutters in the wind as an elder speaks to the children.

pages.text: Back at school, the class made a poster: What we saw, What we think, What we still ask. They thanked the elders, and with the chief’s permission, the community planned to clear the path and put up a sign telling the village’s story. The ghosts were gone, but the story of Old Akokoaso was louder than ever. The end.
